title: Who was the worst monster of the 20th century?
gist: Noah Smith builds a six-factor rubric for ranking regime evil — total deaths, intentionality, willfulness, harm relative to population controlled, unrealized plans, and life for survivors — and applies it to rank Hitler, Imperial Japan, the Khmer Rouge, Stalin and Mao, arguing the exercise matters because real politics forces choices between monsters. He then extends it to the 21st century, putting Sudan's RSF/Janjaweed first, ISIS second and Putin third, with the operative prediction that Putin will not stop waging wars of aggression until he dies or is defeated.

themes.theme: A rubric for ranking regime evil

insights.claim: A defensible ranking of regime evil weighs six factors: total death toll in power, how much was intentional, how much was willful versus accidental, harm relative to the size of the population controlled, atrocities the regime planned but could not accomplish, and what life was like for those who survived.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A transferable scoring framework for assessing present-day regimes on more than casualty counts — useful when judging which authoritarian counterparty is the lesser evil.
insights.locator: some factors we should consider when assessing

insights.claim: Ranking historical monsters is practically relevant because real geopolitics forces choices between them — America had to decide whether allying with Stalin against Hitler was worth it, later formed a quasi-alliance with Mao's China against the Soviet Union, and Syrians in 2016 had to choose between Assad, ISIS and al Qaeda offshoots.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Alliance-of-convenience logic is a live template for how democracies will handle today's autocracies — relative rather than absolute evil drives actual foreign policy.
insights.quote: Sometimes real life forces you to choose between monsters.
insights.locator: The point of ranking evil regimes

insights.claim: The emotional force of mass atrocity decays surprisingly fast: Genghis Khan killed tens of millions but is now invoked as a joke or object of reverence, ironic Chairman Mao posters were dorm decor by the early 2000s, and leftist pundits like Hasan Piker now praise Mao as 'one of the great leaders of this world' without irony.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Historical memory decays on a roughly two-generation clock, which is how ideologies with catastrophic records get rehabilitated and become politically viable again.
insights.quote: By the early 2000s, hipsters in my dorm were already hanging ironic Chairman Mao posters in their rooms.
insights.locator: With time, the emotional power of those events fades

themes.theme: Nazi Germany as a categorical outlier

insights.claim: Hitler's regime ranks first not because the Jewish Holocaust was uniquely horrible relative to other genocides but because it was only the opening phase — Generalplan Ost and the Hunger Plan called for the deliberate slaughter or enslavement of tens of millions more across Russia and Eastern Europe.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Judging a regime by its stated plans rather than its realized body count is the analytical move that changes the ranking — and the same move applies to reading current revanchist doctrines.
insights.locator: #1: Adolf Hitler and the Nazis

insights.claim: Of the 27 million Soviet citizens killed by the Nazis during World War 2, 19 million were civilians, most of whom probably died of hunger and disease driven in large part by a deliberate policy of mass starvation.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Starvation, not combat or camps, was the primary killing mechanism — the reason food systems and siege tactics remain the highest-casualty instruments in modern conflict.
insights.locator: Out of the 27 million Soviet citizens killed

insights.claim: The Nazi state was structurally incapable of stopping at any conquest because it was purpose-built for conquest and genocide, distinguishing it from conquerors like Genghis Khan or Timur who killed in order to subdue and rule rather than to annihilate.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Regimes whose internal logic requires continuous expansion cannot be contained by concession — a test to apply before betting on negotiated settlements.
insights.quote: Hitler’s regime was purpose-built for conquest and genocide — it could only keep killing or die.
insights.locator: And why would Hitler have stopped there?

insights.claim: With an intentional body count of over 30 million and plans for more, the Nazi regime was less like other historical tyrannies and more like an alien armada — which makes the decision to ally with Stalin to defeat it unquestionably correct.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Establishes the threshold at which allying with a lesser monster becomes defensible — the argument later applied to today's coalition choices.
insights.locator: Hitler and the Nazis should thus stand

themes.theme: Imperial Japan as the underrated case

insights.claim: Imperial Japan ranks second and is routinely left off lists of history's worst monsters only because its crimes were committed in a very distributed way — the Imperial Japanese Army was remarkably decentralized and many local commanders carried out atrocities on their own initiative rather than under an official state ideology of race war.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Decentralized atrocity is systematically under-attributed and under-punished, which distorts historical accountability and, by extension, present-day deterrence.
insights.quote: We tend to leave Japan off of the list of “history’s worst monsters”, because these crimes were committed in a very distributed way.
insights.locator: #2: Fascist Japan

insights.claim: Japan killed roughly 14 million Chinese people during its invasion — estimates range from 6 to 20 million — mostly by deliberate starvation or the slaughter of whole towns, used biological weapons to try to kill more, and killed over 10,000 people through human experimentation.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: The magnitude of unresolved Sino-Japanese historical grievance is a persistent input into East Asian security politics and periodic consumer boycotts.
insights.locator: They killed 14 million Chinese people in their invasion

insights.claim: Like the Mongols 700 years earlier, Japanese conquerors were acutely aware of China's larger population and used genocide intentionally as a tool to make China easier to rule.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Population asymmetry as a motive for mass killing is a recurring pattern in occupations — worth noting wherever a smaller power occupies a much larger one.
insights.locator: Like the Mongols 700 years earlier

themes.theme: Per-capita intensity and the Khmer Rouge

insights.claim: The Khmer Rouge rank third despite a total body count of only 1.5 to 3 million because they slaughtered a fifth to a quarter of their own populace — a higher share than any other regime on the list, and possibly in recorded history.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Normalizing atrocity by population controlled reorders the rankings entirely — the same normalization that separates small-state catastrophes from great-power ones.
insights.locator: #3: Pol Pot and the Khmer Rouge

insights.claim: The Khmer Rouge's low absolute toll reflects Cambodia's small population rather than restraint — had they been able to conquer a larger neighbour they probably would have killed more, and their reign was only stopped by a Vietnamese invasion.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Capability, not intent, was the binding constraint — which means external military intervention, not internal collapse, was the operative stopping mechanism.
insights.locator: But the reason they only killed a few million people

themes.theme: Stalin and Mao: brutality without expansionism

insights.claim: Stalin is held responsible for 10 to 20 million deaths, of which perhaps 6 to 10 million starved because of communist agricultural policies, and he deliberately murdered perhaps 3 million political opponents by execution or neglect in gulags.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Baseline numbers for the comparative-evil argument, and a reminder that famine deaths dominate deliberate executions even in the most murderous regimes.
insights.locator: #4: The USSR under Stalin

insights.claim: Stalin's Ukrainian famine differs from Mao's in intent: he probably wanted a famine in Ukraine specifically to reduce the Ukrainian population and make the republic easier to rule.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Intent is the axis that separates catastrophic incompetence from genocide, and it is the axis on which contemporary legal and political judgments actually turn.
insights.locator: But there may have been more to it in Stalin’s case

insights.claim: What kept Stalin ranked below the fascist regimes is that he largely did not try to conquer new territory — he sat on his existing empire, dominated neighbours through proxies, and focused on internal reorganization and personal power, which is precisely what made him palatable as an ally against Hitler.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Territorial ambition, not domestic brutality, is what makes a regime an unacceptable partner — the operative distinction in how the West treats different autocracies today.
insights.locator: What Stalin mostly didn’t do was conquer

insights.claim: Mao is not history's greatest tyrant even though 36 to 40 million died in his Great Famine, because killing tens of millions was never his plan — he kept failing agricultural policies in place after learning they were failing in order to avoid losing face in front of CCP rivals.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Elite face-saving inside closed political systems can be more lethal than malice — a systemic risk factor in any regime where admitting error is career-ending.
insights.quote: But killing tens of millions of his own people was never Mao’s plan.
insights.locator: #5: China under Mao

insights.claim: It was Deng Xiaoping, not Mao, who made modern China great: Mao repeatedly aggrandized himself at China's expense, willfully derailed multiple periods of reform and recovery, and preferred to let the Japanese invaders weaken his Chinese rivals rather than fight them.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Which founder a regime credits for its success signals which policy direction it intends — Mao rehabilitation inside China would be a bearish structural signal.
insights.quote: It was Deng Xiaoping, not Mao, who made modern China great.
insights.locator: Piker is wrong, of course

insights.claim: The very worst atrocities come during wars of conquest, where foreign peoples are dehumanized and armies are given carte blanche, and war itself increases a regime's appetite for further conquest and destruction — so regimes that invade other countries tend to be worse.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Invasion is the single best predictor of escalating atrocity, which argues for pricing tail risk in conflicts the moment a border is crossed.
insights.locator: First of all, the very worst atrocities come during times of war

insights.claim: Communist regimes starved their populations because successful communist revolutions usually began as revolts by agrarian peasantry rather than the proletarian workers Marx envisioned, so in trying to transform agriculture they ended up starving their people.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A structural explanation for why food systems are the recurring failure point of revolutionary regimes — the place to watch when an ideological government restructures agriculture.
insights.quote: Insane agricultural policies were a hallmark of communist economics
insights.locator: Second, communist regimes tended to starve

insights.claim: Communism caused more aggregate human misery than fascism in the 20th century only because fascism did not have time — it was so malignant that external coalitions stopped it quickly, making communism a chronic debilitating disease and fascism more like ebola.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Body counts confound lethality with duration; the acute-versus-chronic distinction is the right way to compare regimes with very different lifespans.
insights.quote: Communism was more like a chronic debilitating disease, while fascism war more like ebola.
insights.locator: So while communism probably caused more aggregate human misery

themes.theme: Worst regimes of the 21st century so far

insights.claim: The worst regime of the 21st century so far is the Sudanese complex of the RSF, Omar al-Bashir and the Janjaweed, responsible for a rolling series of genocides — the first and second Darfur genocides and the Masalit genocide among them.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Sudan is ranked as the century's worst ongoing atrocity yet attracts the least attention — a mismatch that matters for sanctions, commodity flows and humanitarian exposure in the Horn of Africa.
insights.locator: 1. The RSF, Omar al-Bashir, and the Janjaweed

insights.claim: ISIS is the closest recent analogue to the Khmer Rouge, and its total death toll stayed comparatively low precisely because it was so horrible that everyone immediately united to fight and destroy it.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Extreme visible barbarity triggers fast coalition formation, so the most brutal actors are often the shortest-lived — the opposite of what casualty rankings imply.
insights.locator: 2. ISIS

insights.claim: Putin is one of the most aggressive leaders of modern times — starting wars in Georgia and Ukraine and intervening in Syria, with over half a million dead in Ukraine so far — and he will not stop prosecuting wars of aggression until he dies or is defeated.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Rules out a negotiated end to Russian aggression as a base case, which keeps European defence spending, energy security and Russia-risk premia structurally elevated.
insights.quote: It seems clear at this point that he’s not going to stop prosecuting wars of aggression until he dies or is defeated.
insights.locator: 3. Vladimir Putin

insights.claim: Myanmar's Tatmadaw escalated sharply after its 2021 coup against the democratically elected government, putting down protests with extreme brutality and leaving the country an anarchic wasteland with war crimes galore.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: State collapse in Myanmar is a persistent source of regional instability, illicit trade and refugee flows on China's and Thailand's borders.
insights.locator: 5. The Tatmadaw

insights.claim: Today's worst regimes no longer fit the fascism-versus-communism dichotomy that dominated the 20th century — they are motivated instead by Islamism, local ethnic chauvinism, or simple personal lust for power.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Ideology-based country risk models built on 20th-century categories will mis-score modern conflicts; ethnic and personalist drivers are the ones to model now.
insights.locator: They also don’t clearly fit into the “fascism vs. communism” dichotomy

insights.claim: The years 2000 to 2026 have been meaningfully less destructive than the equivalent early stretch of the 20th century, which by 1926 had already produced World War I, the Armenian Genocide, Lenin's purges and the Russian Civil War.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A calibration point against catastrophist narratives: current conflict intensity is historically moderate, which matters when sizing geopolitical tail hedges.
insights.locator: So far, the 21st century has been somewhat less destructive

insights.claim: Indonesia saw robust economic growth under Suharto even as he killed over half a million people for political and ethnic reasons, showing that growth records and atrocity records can coexist in the same regime.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Development performance is no evidence of regime restraint — a caution against treating growth as a proxy for governance quality in emerging-market allocation.
insights.locator: Suharto: Although Indonesia saw robust economic growth

insights.claim: King Leopold II's extractive regime in the Congo killed anywhere from 1.2 to 10 million people, but most of those atrocities occurred in the 19th century and his rule over Congo ended in 1908 — which is why he only rates an honourable mention on a 20th-century list.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Illustrates how period boundaries and estimate ranges — 1.2 to 10 million is nearly an order of magnitude — drive comparative-atrocity conclusions.
insights.locator: King Leopold II: The Belgian king’s extractive regime
